questions.question: Q: What is the difference between an open and a closed question?
questions.correctAnswer: An open question allows free-text answers giving detailed responses; a closed question offers fixed options that are easy to analyse but limit responses.

questions.question: Q: Why should leading questions be avoided?
questions.correctAnswer: Because they bias the results by encouraging a particular answer, making the data unrepresentative of respondents' true views.

questions.question: Q: What is a double-barrelled question?
questions.correctAnswer: A question that asks two things at once, making it unclear which part the respondent is answering, e.g. 'Do you enjoy maths and science?'

questions.question: Q: How can a pilot study improve a questionnaire?
questions.correctAnswer: By identifying unclear questions, missing response options, and practical problems before the main survey, so they can be corrected.

questions.question: Q: Name two ways to increase the response rate of a questionnaire.
questions.correctAnswer: Keep it short and simple; ensure anonymity; offer an incentive; use clear and simple language; send reminders.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response A student writes this question on a questionnaire: 'How many hours of TV do you watch each week? (a) 0–5, (b) 5–10, (c) 10–15, (d) 15+'. Identify two problems and rewrite the question with improved options. <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Problem 1: The response options overlap — someone who watches exactly 5 hours could choose (a) or (b), and 10 hours could be (b) or (c). Problem 2: The upper limit of option (d) is open-ended ('15+'), which makes analysis of the upper range difficult. Improved version: 'How many hours of TV do you watch each week?' (a) 0–4, (b) 5–9, (c) 10–14, (d) 15–19, (e) 20 or more. The intervals are now non-overlapping and exhaustive, covering all possible values.
